candidate.title: Fake Amazon "Product Recall" Refund Text Scam
candidate.summary: Scammers send unexpected texts pretending to be Amazon, claiming an item you bought failed a "quality inspection" or was recalled, and offer a full refund if you click a link — but it's a phishing scam designed to steal your money or personal information.
safetyTips: Don't click links in unexpected texts — and don't respond to them. If you think the message could be legit, contact the company using a phone number, email, or website you know is real, not the info from the text.
Check your Amazon account directly by logging in through the Amazon website or app — don't use the link in the text — to see if there's actually a problem with or recall on anything you've ordered.
Send unwanted texts to 7726 (SPAM) or use your phone's 'report junk' option, then delete the message.
Report any scam you spot to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
candidate.howItWorks: According to the FTC, you get an unexpected text that looks like it's from Amazon. It claims the company did a "routine quality inspection" and an item you recently bought doesn't meet Amazon's standards or has been recalled. The text offers you a full refund and says you don't need to return the item — as long as you click a link to request your money back. But there is no refund. Instead, it's a phishing scam to steal your money or personal information.
redFlags: An unexpected text claiming to be from Amazon about a product recall or failed quality inspection
An offer of a full refund without needing to return the item
A request to click a link to 'request your money back'
Urgency around confirming or claiming a refund via text rather than through the official Amazon app or website
realExamples: FTC Consumer Alert (July 24, 2025) describing texts claiming an Amazon purchase failed a 'routine quality inspection' or was recalled, offering a full refund via a link that is actually a phishing scam.
candidate.source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Scammy texts offering 'refunds' for Amazon purchases," https://www.consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2025/07/scammy-texts-offering-refunds-amazon-purchases

triage.reasoning: This is essentially a smishing/phishing text scam impersonating Amazon with a refund-click lure, which closely overlaps with existing "Smishing Text Message Scam" and "Package Delivery Text Scam" patterns already in the database — same mechanism (unexpected text, link click, phishing for money/personal info) with only the pretext (product recall vs. delivery) differing. It could be argued as a narrow variant worth noting but lacks enough unique mechanism to be a wholly distinct entry.
